sections.title: Chapter goals and early pest disasters

p: After studying this chapter, you should be able to do the following.
list: Define **pest**.
State the four main groups of pests and give an example of each.
Discuss the importance of pest identification in pest control.
List six general pest management methods.
Define **integrated pest management (IPM)**.
List five benefits of using IPM.
Discuss how using one or more control options can improve pest control.
Describe how selectivity and persistence affect chemical controls.
Explain how pest population levels trigger control procedures.
Distinguish between prevention and suppression when developing pest management goals.
Give several reasons why pesticide applications may fail.
Explain the importance of a pesticide's mode of action in managing pesticide resistance.
List two tactics that will minimize the development of pesticide resistance.

p: Civilization has been combating insects and other pests throughout history.
Perhaps the most infamous human catastrophe was the **Black Plague** of Europe, when millions of people in the 14th century died from a mysterious scourge.
Centuries later, it was determined that the cause was a **bacterial disease spread by rat fleas**.
When rats, the normal host animals, were unavailable as a food source, the fleas sought other warm-blooded hosts, including humans.
Although the plague is still present in parts of the world today, controlling rats, other rodents, and fleas can greatly reduce disease incidence.
The destruction of Ireland's potato crop by a fungal disease in the 19th century directly affected the population of the United States.
**Late blight** essentially eliminated potatoes, the staple food crop of Ireland.
Potatoes not destroyed in the field rotted in storage during the winter.
Thousands of Irish starved in the resulting famine, and more than a million migrated to the United States.
Late blight continues to be a major problem of potatoes.
Today it is managed through the use of **resistant cultivars, proper sanitation practices, and fungicides**.

questions.q: What caused the Black Plague of Europe?
choices: A fungal disease spread by rats
A bacterial disease spread by rat fleas
questions.why: Centuries later, the cause was found to be a bacterial disease spread by rat fleas.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT listed as a way late blight of potatoes is managed today?
questions.why: The manual lists resistant cultivars, proper sanitation practices, and fungicides.

questions.q: Ireland's potato famine was caused by an insect pest.
questions.why: It was late blight, a fungal disease.

questions.q: A health department wants fewer plague cases in a region where the plague is still present. What does the manual say can greatly reduce disease incidence?
choices: Controlling rats, other rodents, and fleas
questions.why: Controlling rats, other rodents, and fleas can greatly reduce disease incidence.

questions.q: Plague fleas turned to humans when their normal host animals were unavailable. What were those normal host animals?
questions.why: Rats were the normal hosts. Without them, the fleas sought other warm-blooded hosts, including humans.

sections.title: Malaria, beetles, and what a pest is

p: **Malaria** is a disease caused by the transmission of a parasitic microorganism, a **protozoan**, by **mosquitoes** when they feed on humans.
Historians credit malaria with altering the patterns of human history and causing the collapse of some civilizations.
During World War II, 500,000 soldiers were infected in the South Pacific and African theaters, with 60,000 deaths recorded.
In 2010, malaria cases numbered 219 million, with 660,000 people dying from this debilitating disease.
Antimalarial drugs, insecticide applications, environmental modifications, and mosquito (bed) nets have brought great improvements to fighting this difficult-to-control disease.

In the early 21st century, outbreaks of the native **mountain pine beetle** in the western United States and Canada destroyed more than 4 million acres of lodgepole, ponderosa, Scots, and limber pines.
During this same period, the **emerald ash borer** was accidentally introduced from Asia.
It has destroyed millions of ash trees in the midwestern United States.
Preventive insecticidal treatments are being used to manage these two destructive beetles.
These examples illustrate the enormity and complexity of pest problems.
But what is a pest?
A **pest** is an undesirable organism that injures humans, desirable plants and animals, manufactured products, or natural substances.
Many insects, **pathogens**, plants, mollusks, fish, birds, and a variety of mammals compete for our crops and livestock.
Pathogens are disease-causing organisms, such as viruses, bacteria, or fungi.
Plants that are pests are known as **weeds**.
Mollusks are slugs and snails, and the mammals range from mice to deer.
In addition, some pests destroy clothing, furniture, and buildings.
Some reduce the beauty and recreational value of the landscape, and some invade our homes during the winter months.
As the battle between humans and pests continues over time, so will innovative methods of control.

questions.q: Which is the manual's definition of a pest?
choices: Any insect found on a crop
An undesirable organism that injures humans, desirable plants and animals, manufactured products, or natural substances
Any organism that is not native to an area
An organism that has become resistant to pesticides
questions.why: That is the manual's definition, word for word.

questions.q: Type the definition of a pest.
questions.answer: An undesirable organism that injures humans, desirable plants and animals, manufactured products, or natural substances.
questions.why: Know all four things a pest injures: humans, desirable plants and animals, manufactured products, and natural substances.

questions.q: Malaria is caused by which kind of organism, transmitted by mosquitoes?
questions.why: Malaria is caused by a parasitic microorganism, a protozoan, spread by mosquitoes when they feed on humans.

questions.q: The emerald ash borer is a native beetle of the western United States.
questions.why: The emerald ash borer was accidentally introduced from Asia. The native one is the mountain pine beetle.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT listed as having improved the fight against malaria?
questions.why: The manual lists antimalarial drugs, insecticide applications, environmental modifications, and bed nets.

p: For many centuries, the causes of crop failures and human and animal diseases were shrouded in mystery.
The first pest control measures were crude: weeds were pulled, rats were clubbed, and beetles were plucked from foliage.

list: Burning to control weeds, diseases, and insects, in 950 B.C.
Egyptians placing fishnets over beds to prevent mosquito bites, in 440 B.C.
Romans using rat-proof grain storage bins, in 13 B.C.

p: The first known use of **natural enemies** is credited to **Arabian growers**, in 1000 A.D.
Arab farmers moved colonies of a predaceous ant species from nearby mountains to an oasis to control pest ants that were damaging their date palms.

list: The earliest use of chemicals as pesticides dates back to **2500 B.C.**, when the **Sumerians** used **sulfur** compounds to control mites and insects.
The **Chinese** used **mercury and arsenic** compounds in 500 B.C. to control body lice.
Early plant-derived insecticides included **hellebore** to control body lice, **nicotine** to control aphids, and **pyrethrins** to control a wide variety of insects.

p: In France during the late 19th century, a farmer sprayed a mixture of **lime and copper sulfate** on grapevines to deter passers-by from picking the grapes.
The farmer found that the mixture also controlled **downy mildew**, a serious fungal disease of grapes.
Later named **Bordeaux mixture**, it remains a widely used fungicide worldwide.
Until the 1940s, pest control chemicals were derived from plants and inorganic compounds.
During World War II, the synthetic chemical **DDT** saved many Allied soldiers from insect-transmitted diseases.
Synthetic pesticides launched the modern-day chemical industry and a new era in pest control.

body.box: Why pesticides became the primary means of solving pest problems
list: They were effective.
They were relatively inexpensive.
They provided season-long crop protection.
They could be used with fertilizers and other production practices.

p: Modern pesticides achieved wide acceptance following their successful use in agriculture and for human health.

questions.q: What is the earliest recorded use of chemicals as pesticides?
choices: Sumerians using sulfur compounds in 2500 B.C.
Chinese using mercury and arsenic compounds in 500 B.C.
Romans using rat-proof grain bins in 13 B.C.
questions.why: The Sumerians used sulfur compounds against mites and insects in 2500 B.C.

questions.q: Bordeaux mixture, still a widely used fungicide, is a mixture of:
questions.why: A French farmer sprayed lime and copper sulfate on grapevines and found it also controlled downy mildew.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a reason the manual gives for pesticides becoming the primary means of solving pest problems?
choices: They had no effect on the environment
questions.why: The four reasons: effective, relatively inexpensive, season-long protection, and usable with fertilizers and other practices.

questions.q: Which early plant-derived insecticide was used to control aphids?
questions.why: Hellebore was for body lice, nicotine for aphids, and pyrethrins for a wide variety of insects.

questions.q: Long ago, farmers moved colonies of predaceous ants to an oasis to protect date palms from pest ants. What was this the first known use of?
questions.why: The first known use of natural enemies is credited to Arabian growers, in 1000 A.D.

p: In recent years, some drawbacks of heavy dependence on pesticides have become increasingly apparent.
**Pesticide resistance** to DDT was documented in **1947**.
Since that time, hundreds of insects have become resistant to one or more pesticides.
Most notable is the **Colorado potato beetle**, which has developed resistance to every major group of insecticides, greatly complicating pest management efforts.
Resistance also has arisen in many weeds and plant pathogens in agricultural production.
In **1962**, **Rachel Carson** graphically illustrated the impact of increasing pesticide use on the environment.
Her book, **Silent Spring**, focused on DDT and other **chlorinated hydrocarbons** because of their long residual activity and persistence in the environment.
Although these characteristics contributed to their effectiveness, chlorinated hydrocarbons also accumulated in the fatty tissue of some animals, especially those higher in the food chain.
This is called **bioaccumulation**.
In certain situations, some organisms accumulated chemical residues in higher concentrations than those found in the food organisms they consumed.
This is called **biomagnification**.

Ecologists refer to a **food chain** as the sequence of animals feeding in the natural environment, where a particular plant, animal, or microorganism is eaten by an animal that is in turn eaten by another animal.
Animals at each level normally consume individuals from the previous level.
Figure 1.1 shows how biomagnification of a pesticide can occur in a food chain.
Organisms with pesticides in their tissues are eaten by fish, which are in turn eaten by birds.
The birds at the top of the food chain accumulate the highest concentration of pesticide residues.
Since the publication of Silent Spring, the United States has experienced a level of environmental awareness unequal to any other period in history.
The U.S. **Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)** was created in **1970** by Congress to implement laws passed to protect the environment and the health of humans and other animals.
In **1972**, EPA **banned the use of DDT** in the United States.
Regulatory action has since been taken against many chemicals thought to pose significant environmental and health hazards.

figures.title: Figure 1.1: Biomagnification in the food chain
explain: DDT concentration, in parts per million, goes from .000003 in water, to .04 in planktonic algae, .20 in zooplankton, 2.0 in fish, and 20.00 in fish-eating birds.
The figure labels this a concentration increase of 10 million times.

questions.q: What is biomagnification?
choices: Organisms accumulating chemical residues in higher concentrations than those found in the food organisms they consumed
A pest's ability to tolerate a pesticide that once controlled it
A pesticide breaking down in storage
Spreading a pesticide over a large area
questions.why: That is biomagnification. Bioaccumulation is buildup in fatty tissue, especially in animals higher in the food chain.

questions.q: In Figure 1.1, which level has the highest DDT concentration?
questions.why: Fish-eating birds are at the top of the food chain, at 20.00 parts per million.

questions.q: In what year did EPA ban the use of DDT in the United States?
questions.why: 1947: DDT resistance documented. 1962: Silent Spring. 1970: EPA created. 1972: DDT banned.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT true of DDT and other chlorinated hydrocarbons, according to the manual?
choices: They accumulated in the fatty tissue of some animals
They break down within a few hours
questions.why: Silent Spring focused on them because of their long residual activity and persistence.

questions.q: The Colorado potato beetle has developed resistance to every major group of insecticides.
questions.why: The manual calls it the most notable example of resistance.

sections.title: The four main groups of pests

p: There are four main groups of pest organisms: **weeds, invertebrate animals, pathogens, and vertebrate animals**.

body.box: The four main groups of pests
ol: **Invertebrates**: insects, mites, ticks, spiders, snails, and slugs.
**Disease agents or pathogens**: bacteria, viruses, fungi, nematodes (roundworms), mycoplasmas (parasitic microorganisms), and other microorganisms.
**Vertebrates**: birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish, and rodents and other mammals.

p: Never classify an organism as a pest until it is clearly determined to be one.
Be certain any injury or observed damage is actually due to the identified organism and not to some other cause.
Some plants, for example, can be damaged by factors in the environment.
These factors include **weather extremes, air pollutants, road salt, and inadequate or excessive fertilization**.
This damage may be mistaken for that caused by living pests.

questions.q: Name the four main groups of pests.
questions.ref: p. 4, 'The Four Main Groups of Pests'
questions.why: Weeds, invertebrates, pathogens (disease agents), and vertebrates.

questions.q: Nematodes (roundworms) are listed in which group of pests?
questions.ref: p. 4, 'The Four Main Groups of Pests'
questions.why: The manual lists nematodes with the disease agents or pathogens, not the invertebrates.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT listed as an invertebrate pest?
questions.ref: p. 4, 'The Four Main Groups of Pests'
questions.why: Amphibians are vertebrates.

questions.q: Shrubs along a highway turn brown after winter. You find no insects or disease. What should you consider before calling it a pest problem?
choices: Damage from road salt, an environmental factor
questions.why: Weather extremes, air pollutants, road salt, and fertilization problems can look like pest damage.

questions.q: You should classify an organism as a pest as soon as you find it on a damaged plant.
questions.why: Never classify an organism as a pest until it is clearly determined to be one.

p: The first step in pest management is to **accurately identify the pest**.

Once the pest is identified, applicators can learn about its life cycle, behavior, characteristic damage, factors that favor its development, susceptible life stage or stages, and known control methods.
Misidentification and lack of accurate information could cause **pest control failure**.
To identify an organism, consult reference materials: **identification books, Extension bulletins, field guides, and online identification keys** that contain pictures and biological information.
If you cannot pinpoint a specific plant or animal, take or send the specimen to a **university diagnostic lab** or a **local pest management specialist**.
Collect several specimens, if possible.
Ask the specialist to recommend the best way to collect and send samples.
It may be difficult to identify small insects and most mites, nematodes, and plant pathogens.
Accurate identification requires the use of a **hand lens or microscope, special tests, or careful damage analysis**.
Often the pest's **host**, the animal or plant on which an organism lives, and its **location** are important clues in making a correct identification.
Information on the environmental conditions where you collect pests, and the time of year of collection, also provide clues to the pest's identity.
Pest species have different physical forms depending on the **life cycle stage** or the **time of year**.
Weed seedlings, for example, often do not resemble the mature plant.
Many insect species undergo changes in appearance as they develop from eggs through immature stages to the adult form.
Pests may leave signs of their presence or damage that will help you determine what they are.
Birds and rodents often build characteristic nests.
The type of feeding damage and excrement can help you identify many insects.
Burrows, gnaw marks, tracks, trails in the grass, and/or feces are often characteristic of certain mammals.
Weeds may have unique flowers, seeds, or fruits, or unusual growth habits.
Fungi and other pathogens often cause specific types of damage, deformation, or color changes in host tissues.

questions.q: What is the first step in pest management?
questions.why: Identification comes first. Misidentification could cause pest control failure.

questions.q: You find tiny mites on a crop and cannot tell what they are. What does the manual say to do?
choices: Spray a broad-spectrum pesticide to be safe
Take or send specimens to a university diagnostic lab or a local pest management specialist
Treat them the same as weeds
questions.why: Collect several specimens if possible, and ask the specialist how to collect and send them.

questions.q: In pest identification, what is the pest's host?
choices: The person who reported the pest
The animal or plant on which an organism lives
A natural enemy that eats the pest
The building where the pest was found
questions.why: The host and the location are important clues for a correct identification.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT listed as a sign often characteristic of certain mammals?
questions.why: Color changes in host tissues point to fungi and other pathogens.

questions.q: Name a tool the manual says you may need to identify small insects, mites, nematodes, and plant pathogens.
questions.why: A hand lens or microscope, special tests, or careful damage analysis.

p: Once a pest problem is identified, you can begin planning how to manage the pest.
Determine what management methods are available and the benefits and limitations of each.
Select methods that are most effective in controlling the pest yet **least harmful to people and the environment**.
**Abiotic factors** are natural control measures within the environment that injure or destroy plants and animals, including pests.
They include climatic factors, such as wind, temperature, sunshine, and rain.
They include air or water pollution.
And they include topographic features, such as rivers, lakes, and mountains, that can affect pest movement.
If such natural controls do not hold pests in check, humans must intervene and apply pest management tactics.
**Natural controls**.
**Applied controls**, which are:

figures.title: Diagram: pest management methods at a glance
explain: When natural controls do not hold pests in check, people apply one or more of the six applied controls.

questions.q: What are abiotic factors?
choices: Natural control measures in the environment, such as weather, pollution, and topography, that injure or destroy plants and animals
Natural enemies such as predators and parasites
Government programs that stop the spread of pests
questions.why: Abiotic factors are natural controls: climate, air or water pollution, and topographic features.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the six applied pest controls?
questions.why: Abiotic factors are natural controls, not applied controls.

questions.q: List the six applied pest control methods.
questions.answer: Biological, chemical, cultural, genetic, mechanical/physical, and regulatory
questions.why: Biological, chemical, cultural, genetic, mechanical/physical, and regulatory.

questions.q: A mountain range keeps a pest from moving into a valley. What kind of control is that?
choices: A natural control, an abiotic factor
questions.why: Topographic features like rivers, lakes, and mountains are abiotic factors that can affect pest movement.

questions.q: When choosing pest management methods, select those most effective against the pest yet least harmful to people and the environment.
questions.why: That is the selection rule in the manual.

p: In an undisturbed ecosystem, most organisms have one or more natural enemies or competitors that keep them from developing into large, damaging populations.
When an organism is removed from one ecosystem to another, this natural check-and-balance is disturbed.
The organism can become a pest in the new geographical area, especially when its natural enemies do not accompany it to the new location.
One pest management method involves reuniting the introduced pest with its natural enemies.
**Biological control** is the use of **natural enemies**, which are **predators, parasites, pathogens, and competitors**, to control pests and their damage.
These biological control, or **biocontrol**, agents are being used successfully to manage certain insect, mite, fungal, fish, and weed pests.

Once suitable natural enemies from the native home of an introduced pest are located, extensive testing and evaluation are necessary to ensure that these natural enemies will not become pests themselves in the new environment.
Laws and regulations strictly control the importation of all organisms, including biological control agents, into the United States.
The selected natural enemies are imported, reared, and released.
If successful, these biocontrol agents become established within large areas.
Over time, they will lower target pest populations for long periods with **no further human intervention**.
A second biological control technique is the **mass release** of large numbers of natural enemies into fields, orchards, greenhouses, or other locations to control specific pests.
Because this method usually does not yield long-term results, the natural enemies must be **released periodically**.
For example, **predatory mites** are used to control plant-feeding **spider mites**.
**Parasitic wasps** are used to manage specific pests.
**Praying mantids, lady beetles, and lacewings** are used as **general predators** in a garden or greenhouse.
Nematodes and fungi are being studied as biological control agents for certain weeds and insects.
Another aspect of biological control is to maintain healthy populations of **native natural enemies**.
This could mean planting crops or groundcovers to ensure a diverse plant community of pollen and nectar sources for adult insects.
This method also requires careful selection and use of pesticides that are less toxic to natural enemies.
Additionally, applicators should apply pesticides at **lower-than-label rates**, if recommended and effective, to lessen the impact on natural enemies.

questions.q: Which statement about biological control methods is **true**?
choices: Modifying the environment to enhance natural enemies is recommended in biological control.
Biological control involves importing exotic pests to control natural enemies.
Using several cultural practices and a wide variety of pesticides works best in biological control.
questions.ref: Review question 3, p. 17. Answer in the text: p. 6, 'Biological Control'
questions.why: Keeping native natural enemies healthy, for example with pollen and nectar plants, is biological control. B has it backwards.

questions.q: Biological control is the use of:
choices: Natural enemies, such as predators, parasites, pathogens, and competitors
questions.why: Biological control uses natural enemies to control pests and their damage.

questions.q: A greenhouse grower releases predatory mites every few weeks to control spider mites. Why must the releases be repeated?
choices: Mass release usually does not yield long-term results
Spider mites become resistant to predatory mites
questions.why: Because mass release usually does not give long-term results, natural enemies must be released periodically.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT listed as a general predator used in a garden or greenhouse?
questions.why: Spider mites are the pest that predatory mites control.

questions.q: Natural enemies brought in for an introduced pest need extensive testing to make sure they will not become pests themselves.
questions.why: Testing and evaluation make sure they will not become pests in the new environment.

questions.q: How can an applicator help keep native natural enemies healthy?
choices: Apply pesticides on a fixed schedule
Use pesticides that are less toxic to natural enemies, and lower-than-label rates if recommended and effective
Use the highest labeled rate to kill pests fast
questions.why: Careful pesticide selection and lower-than-label rates, if recommended and effective, lessen the impact on natural enemies.

p: **Chemical control** is the pest management method that involves using **naturally derived and/or synthetic chemicals** to manage pests.
These chemicals are often called pesticides.

A **pesticide** is any material that is applied to plants, soil, water, harvested crops, structures, clothing and furnishings, or animals to **kill, attract, repel, or regulate or interrupt the growth and mating of pests**, or to **regulate plant growth**.
Pesticides often play a key role in pest management programs and may often be the only known control method for a given pest.
Major benefits of pesticides are their **effectiveness**, the **speed and ease** of controlling pests, and their **reasonable cost** compared with other control options.
Pesticides include a wide assortment of chemicals with specialized names and functions.
They are often grouped according to the type of pest they control.

body.box: Pesticides grouped by the pest they control
list: **Avicides** control or repel pest birds.
**Bactericides** control bacteria.
**Chemosterilants** sterilize insects or pest vertebrates.
**Defoliants** cause leaves (foliage) to drop from plants.
**Desiccants** promote drying or loss of moisture from plant tissues and insects.
**Disinfectants** (antimicrobials) control microorganisms.
**Fungicides** control fungi.
**Growth regulators** alter the growth or development of a plant or animal.
**Herbicides** control weeds.
**Insecticides** control insects and related arthropods.
**Miticides** (acaricides) control mites.
**Molluscicides** control snails and slugs.
**Nematicides** control nematodes (roundworms).
**Ovicides** destroy eggs.
**Pheromones** attract insects.
**Piscicides** control pest fish.
**Predacides** control predatory vertebrates, for example, coyotes.
**Repellents** repel insects, mites, ticks, pest vertebrates, invertebrates, birds, and mammals.
**Rodenticides** control rodents.

questions.q: Which type of pesticide controls mites?
questions.why: Miticides, also called acaricides, control mites.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT part of the manual's definition of a pesticide?
choices: Material applied to attract or repel pests
Material applied to regulate plant growth
Material applied only to crops grown for food
questions.why: A pesticide can be applied to plants, soil, water, harvested crops, structures, clothing and furnishings, or animals.

questions.q: Coyotes are killing a rancher's sheep. Which type of pesticide is made to control predatory vertebrates like coyotes?
questions.why: Predacides control predatory vertebrates, for example, coyotes.

questions.q: What are the major benefits of pesticides named in the manual?
choices: Effectiveness, speed and ease of control, and reasonable cost
questions.why: Effectiveness, speed and ease of controlling pests, and reasonable cost compared with other options.

questions.q: What do molluscicides control?
questions.why: Molluscicides control snails and slugs.

p: Each group of pesticides includes several **classes** or **families**.
For example, the classes of insecticides include the organophosphates, organochlorines, carbamates, pyrethroids, botanicals, insecticidal soaps, and microbials, among others.
The pesticides within a particular class have similar chemical structures or properties, or share a common **mode of action** or **site of action**.
**Mode of action** is how they kill the pest.
**Site of action** is the specific biological system affected within the pest.
The various classes of chemicals work in different ways and present different risks and problems.
Some chemicals are called **selective pesticides** because they are toxic to some pests but have little or no effect on others.
For example, certain selective herbicides control broadleaf weeds but not grasses, and ovicides kill only the eggs of certain insects and mites.
In contrast, **fumigants are nonselective** and will kill a wide variety of pests: fungi, insects, weeds, nematodes, and other organisms.
**Nonselective herbicides** control any susceptible plant, given a sufficient dose.
Pesticides may move in various ways after they contact a host.
**Systemic pesticides** are absorbed and translocated within a plant or animal.
Systemic herbicides are absorbed through leaves or roots and are then transported within the treated plant.
Similarly, systemic insecticides can be eaten by or injected into livestock to control insect pests.
By contrast, **contact pesticides** are not absorbed by treated plants or animals.
These pesticides must directly touch the pest or a site the pest frequents to be effective.
Pesticides also vary in their **persistence**, or how long they remain active to control pests.
Some **residual pesticides** control pests for weeks, months, or even years.
Others provide only short-term control, sometimes lasting only a few hours.

figures.title: Figure 1.2: Systemic and contact pesticides on treated plants
explain: On the left, a systemic pesticide is absorbed and moves inside the plant.
On the right, a contact pesticide stays on the surface of the plant.

questions.q: What is a selective pesticide?
choices: One that is toxic to some pests but has little or no effect on others
One that kills a wide variety of pests
One that stays active for years
One that must touch the pest directly
questions.why: Selective pesticides are toxic to some pests but have little or no effect on others.

questions.q: A rancher controls insect pests on cattle with an insecticide the animals eat or that is injected into them. What kind of insecticide is this?
questions.why: Systemic insecticides can be eaten by or injected into livestock to control insect pests.

questions.q: What is the difference between mode of action and site of action?
choices: Mode of action is how the pesticide kills the pest; site of action is the specific biological system affected within the pest
Mode of action is where it is applied; site of action is how long it lasts
Mode of action is the label code; site of action is where the pest lives
questions.why: Mode of action is how they kill the pest. Site of action is the specific biological system affected.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the insecticide classes named in the manual?
questions.why: Avicides are a pesticide group for birds, not a class of insecticides.

questions.q: What is a pesticide's persistence?
questions.answer: How long it remains active to control pests
questions.why: Persistence is how long a pesticide remains active to control pests.

p: **Cultural controls** are practices that reduce pest **establishment, reproduction, dispersal, and survival**.
Cultural practices and **sanitation** are two examples of cultural control.
Many cultural practices affect pest survival.
**Mowing, irrigation, aeration, and fertilization** are all important ways of producing healthy turf and preventing pest buildup and damage.

In agricultural production, **cultivation, selection of crop plant varieties, timing of planting and harvesting, irrigation management and timing, crop rotation, and the use of trap crops** help decrease populations of weeds, microorganisms, insects, mites, and other pests.
**Cultivation** is one of the most important ways to control weeds.
It is also used to manage some insects and other soil-inhabiting pests.
Plows, disks, mowers, cultivators, and bed conditioners destroy weeds or control their growth.
These tools also disrupt soil conditions suitable for the survival of some microorganisms and insects.
Weeds also can be managed by **mulching**, with plastic, straw, shredded bark, or wood chips, and by using **cover crops**.
**Sanitation** involves eliminating the necessities important to a pest's survival, such as **food, water, or shelter**.

In crop production, sanitation includes such practices as removing weeds that harbor pest insects or rodents, eliminating weed plants before they produce seed, destroying diseased plant material or crop residues, and keeping field borders or surrounding areas free of pests and pest breeding sites.
**Animal manure management** is an effective sanitation practice used to prevent or reduce fly problems in poultry and livestock operations.
Mosquitoes can be controlled by **draining standing water**.
Closed garbage containers and frequent garbage pickup eliminate food sources for flies, cockroaches, wasps, and rodents.
Removing soil, trash, and wood debris from around and under buildings reduces termite and fungal rot damage.

questions.q: Which statement about cultural control practices is **true**?
choices: They reduce pest establishment, reproduction, and survival.
They use naturally derived and/or synthesized chemicals to control pests.
They involve the release of parasites and predators found in foreign countries.
questions.ref: Review question 5, p. 17. Answer in the text: p. 7, 'Cultural Control'
questions.why: B describes chemical control and C describes biological control.

questions.q: Cultural controls are practices that:
choices: Reduce pest establishment, reproduction, dispersal, and survival
Use natural enemies to control pests
Use laws to stop pest movement
questions.why: Cultural controls reduce pest establishment, reproduction, dispersal, and survival.

questions.q: A poultry operation has a fly problem. Which sanitation practice does the manual name for this?
questions.why: Animal manure management prevents or reduces fly problems in poultry and livestock operations.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a cultural control practice named in the manual?
questions.why: Quarantine is regulatory control.

questions.q: What does the manual call one of the most important ways to control weeds?
questions.why: Cultivation is one of the most important ways to control weeds.

questions.q: A homeowner has termite and fungal rot damage. Which sanitation step does the manual say reduces this?
choices: Removing soil, trash, and wood debris from around and under buildings
questions.why: Removing soil, trash, and wood debris from around and under buildings reduces termite and fungal rot damage.

p: Sometimes plants and animals can be **bred or selected to resist** specific pest problems.
For example, certain livestock breeds are selected for physical characteristics that prevent attack by some pests or provide physiological resistance to disease or parasitic organisms.
Certain plant varieties are naturally resistant to insects, pathogens, or nematodes.
Many plants actually repel various types of pests, and some contain toxic substances.
Plant resistance to insect pests can sometimes be achieved by transferring genetic material from certain insect-destroying microorganisms to hybrid seed.
Genetic control has been widely used in the past and may be an effective tool in the future, especially when combined with new gene manipulation techniques.

list: **Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt)** corn and potatoes.
Herbicide-resistant corn, for example, Roundup Ready corn and Liberty Link corn.
Herbicide-resistant cotton, for example, Roundup Ready cotton.
Herbicide-resistant soybean, for example, Roundup Ready soybean.

p: The plant is **genetically modified** through molecular techniques to add a small amount of genetic material from other organisms.
The incorporated genetic traits provide **protection from pests**, **tolerance to herbicides**, or an **improvement in quality**.
For example, **Bt crops produce a protein that kills caterpillars**.

questions.q: Making use of plant varieties that are naturally resistant to insect feeding is an example of which type of pest management method?
questions.ref: Review question 2, p. 17. Answer in the text: p. 8, 'Genetic Control'
questions.why: Plant varieties naturally resistant to insects, pathogens, or nematodes are genetic control.

questions.q: Bt corn is an example of which kind of pest control?
questions.why: The manual lists Bt corn and potatoes as examples of genetic control.

questions.q: What does the protein produced by Bt crops do?
questions.why: Bt crops produce a protein that kills caterpillars.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT an example of genetic control in the manual?
questions.why: Bordeaux mixture is a fungicide, which is chemical control.

questions.q: Certain livestock breeds are selected for physical characteristics that prevent attack by some pests.
questions.why: Some breeds are selected to prevent attack or to resist disease or parasitic organisms.

questions.q: A seed company transfers genetic material from an insect-destroying microorganism into hybrid seed so the crop resists insect pests. What kind of control is this?
questions.why: Building pest resistance into the plant itself is genetic control.

p: Mechanical and physical controls can **kill a pest directly** or **make its environment unsuitable**.
**Rodent traps** are examples of mechanical control.
Several types of traps are commonly used.
Some kill animals that come across them; others snare animals that are then relocated or destroyed.
Traps can be mechanical devices or sticky surfaces, some with **pheromones** incorporated to increase trapping efficiency.
**Physical controls** include mulches for weed management, steam soil sterilization for disease control, deer fences, screens to keep insects out, and cloth mesh to exclude birds from fruit trees.
Another example is **sealing cracks, crevices, and other small openings** in buildings to exclude insects, rodents, bats, birds, and squirrels.
A **band of sticky material** painted around tree trunks prevents crawling insects from reaching the tree's leaves.
Pests living in enclosed areas may sometimes be suppressed by altering physical and environmental conditions, such as **water, air movement, temperature, light, and humidity**.
**Refrigeration**, for example, protects stored food products, furs, and other items from insect pests.
Lowered temperatures kill the insects, cause them to stop feeding, and prevent egg hatch or development.
Installing **bright lights in attics** sometimes discourages bats from roosting there.
**Lowering the humidity** of stored grains and other food products reduces damage from molds and some insects.
**Increasing air movement in greenhouses** often helps to prevent fungal diseases from developing on plants.

questions.q: Using barriers to prevent pests from getting into an area is an example of which type of pest management method?
questions.ref: Review question 1, p. 17. Answer in the text: p. 8, 'Mechanical/Physical Control'
questions.why: Fences, screens, mesh, and sealed openings that keep pests out are mechanical/physical controls.

questions.q: Sealing cracks and crevices and small openings in buildings is an example of which type of pest management method?
questions.ref: Review question 4, p. 17. Answer in the text: p. 8, 'Mechanical/Physical Control'
questions.why: Sealing cracks, crevices, and small openings to exclude pests is a physical control.

questions.q: Rodent traps are an example of:
questions.why: The manual names rodent traps as examples of mechanical control.

questions.q: Bats are roosting in an attic. Which physical control does the manual say sometimes discourages them?
choices: Installing bright lights in the attic
questions.why: Installing bright lights in attics sometimes discourages bats from roosting there.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a physical control listed in the manual?
questions.why: Crop rotation is a cultural control.

questions.q: Increasing air movement in greenhouses often helps prevent fungal diseases from developing on plants.
questions.why: Altering air movement is one of the physical and environmental conditions you can change.

questions.q: Refrigeration protects stored products from insects. Name one thing lowered temperatures do to the insects.
questions.why: Lowered temperatures kill the insects, stop their feeding, and prevent egg hatch or development.

p: Some pest problems cannot be controlled successfully at a local level or by individuals.
These problems are caused by pests that seriously endanger **public health** or are likely to cause **widespread damage** to agricultural crops or animals, forests, or ornamental plants.
**Quarantine** or **eradication** programs directed by governmental agencies according to federal and state laws target the introduction and spread of such pests.
**Quarantine** is a pest control process designed to **prevent entry of certain pests into pest-free areas**.
Some states maintain inspection stations at all major entry points to intercept pests or materials that might harbor pests.
Regulatory agencies monitor airports and ocean ports.
Quarantine also prevents movement of designated pests **within a state**.
Identified items being shipped from a quarantine area must be treated to destroy pests before shipment.
Nursery stock, plant cuttings, seed shipments, and budding and grafting material are also regulated to prevent the spread of pests.
**Eradication** is the **elimination of a pest from a designated area**.
Often, these pests are under quarantine restrictions.
When eradication is required, the geographical extent of pest infestation is determined and control measures are taken to eliminate this pest from the defined area.
Procedures may include an **area-wide spraying program, releasing sterile insects, and intensive monitoring** for pests within and around the borders of the infested area.
Government agencies are authorized to destroy weeds and plants that cause fire hazards, harbor harmful pathogens or animals, or are noxious to people or livestock in and around agricultural areas.
Similar authority applies to diseased or infected livestock or poultry, and to weeds and nuisance plants in residential, commercial, and industrial areas.
**Mosquito abatement** is an important pest control function undertaken to protect public health.
Mosquito abatement laws allow state agencies to **drain or treat standing water** that provides breeding sites for mosquitoes.

questions.q: Monitoring pests at airports and ocean ports that pose a serious threat to public health or widespread damage to crops or animals is an example of which type of pest management method?
questions.ref: Review question 6, p. 17. Answer in the text: p. 9, 'Regulatory Control'
questions.why: Agencies monitoring airports and ocean ports is quarantine, a regulatory control.

questions.q: What is quarantine?
choices: A pest control process designed to prevent entry of certain pests into pest-free areas
The elimination of a pest from a designated area
questions.why: Quarantine keeps certain pests out of pest-free areas, and also stops their movement within a state.

questions.q: What is eradication?
choices: The elimination of a pest from a designated area
Reducing pests below the economic injury level
Preventing pests from entering an area
questions.why: Eradication is the elimination of a pest from a designated area.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT listed as a possible eradication procedure?
choices: Intensive monitoring in and around the infested area
questions.why: Trap crops are a cultural control.

questions.q: A nursery wants to ship plant cuttings out of a quarantine area. What must happen first?
choices: The items must be treated to destroy pests before shipment
Nothing; quarantine only applies at state borders
The nursery must release sterile insects
questions.why: Identified items shipped from a quarantine area must be treated to destroy pests before shipment.

questions.q: Mosquito abatement laws allow state agencies to drain or treat standing water that provides breeding sites for mosquitoes.
questions.why: Mosquito abatement is done to protect public health.

p: Pesticide use is a significant factor in food and fiber production, forestry, turf and landscape maintenance, and public health.
In recent years, pest management has shifted from relying heavily on pesticides to using an integrated approach based on **pest assessment, decision-making, and evaluation**.
This pest management approach has benefited pest managers and the environment, decreased pesticide use, and reduced the occurrence of pesticide resistance in pest populations.
**Integrated pest management** is a balanced, tactical approach to pest control.
It defines ways to **anticipate pest outbreaks and prevent pest damage**.
IPM is a pest management strategy that uses a wide range of pest control methods, for example, cultural, biological, mechanical, and chemical, or tactics such as **sanitation and exclusion**.
The goal of this strategy is to prevent pests from reaching damaging levels with the **least risk to the environment**.
Such pest management programs enable the specialist to make intelligent, **site-specific** decisions about control.
A pest management strategy that utilizes a wide range of pest control methods or tactics.
The goal of this strategy is to prevent pests from reaching **economically or aesthetically damaging levels** with the least risk to the environment.

ol: IPM helps to keep a balanced ecosystem.
IPM maintains a good public image.

questions.q: What is the goal of IPM?
choices: Prevent pests from reaching economically or aesthetically damaging levels with the least risk to the environment
Eliminate every pest from a site
Use pesticides on a regular schedule
questions.why: That is the goal stated in the IPM definition box.

questions.q: Define integrated pest management (IPM).
questions.answer: A pest management strategy that utilizes a wide range of pest control methods or tactics to prevent pests from reaching economically or aesthetically damaging levels with the least risk to the environment.
questions.why: A strategy using a wide range of methods or tactics to prevent damaging pest levels with the least risk to the environment.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the five reasons to practice IPM?
choices: IPM helps keep a balanced ecosystem
IPM maintains a good public image
IPM guarantees pests will never return
questions.why: The five: balanced ecosystem, pesticides can be ineffective, saves money, healthy environment, good public image.

questions.q: In recent years, pest management has shifted toward relying more heavily on pesticides.
questions.why: It shifted away from heavy reliance on pesticides, toward an integrated approach.

questions.q: A school wants a pest program based on pest assessment, decision-making, and evaluation, using sanitation and exclusion along with other methods. What approach is this?
questions.why: IPM is an integrated approach based on pest assessment, decision-making, and evaluation.

p: **IPM helps preserve a balanced ecosystem.**
Every ecosystem, made up of living things and their nonliving environment, has a balance: the actions of one kind of organism usually affect other species.
Introducing chemicals into the ecosystem can change this balance, destroying certain species and allowing other species, sometimes other pests, to dominate.
Unfortunately, pesticides can kill **beneficial insects** that consume pests, leaving few natural pest control mechanisms.
**Pesticides can be ineffective.**
Chemical pesticides do not always work.
Many common weeds, insects, and disease-causing fungi have developed a resistance to pesticides.
Furthermore, pests may survive if the chemical **does not reach them, is washed off, or is applied improperly**.
**IPM can save money.**
A good IPM program can prevent crop loss and landscape or structural damage caused by pests.
IPM may also avoid the cost of purchasing unnecessary pesticides.
Moreover, IPM can reduce the costs of treating chronic conditions such as **asthma** by controlling disease triggers.
**IPM promotes a healthy environment.**
Using IPM strategies helps reduce environmental injury.
Using fewer pesticides lowers the risk that persistent chemicals may harm living creatures and contaminate **groundwater**.
It also lessens the need to dispose of containers and unused pesticides.
**IPM helps maintain a good public image.**
IPM is a well-known strategy that is requested in many areas of society.
IPM is used to grow food, manage turf and ornamentals, protect homes and businesses, manage school grounds, and safeguard the health of humans, pets, and livestock.

questions.q: How can pesticides upset a balanced ecosystem?
choices: They can kill beneficial insects that consume pests, leaving few natural pest control mechanisms
They always increase the number of natural enemies
They only affect the target pest
They make weeds grow more slowly
questions.why: Chemicals can destroy certain species and let others, sometimes other pests, dominate.

questions.q: An apartment manager says IPM costs too much. According to the manual, how can IPM save money?
choices: By preventing damage, avoiding unnecessary pesticide purchases, and reducing costs of treating conditions like asthma
By always using the cheapest pesticide
questions.why: IPM prevents loss and damage, avoids unnecessary pesticides, and controls asthma triggers.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a reason the manual gives for why pesticides can be ineffective?
choices: The chemical does not reach the pest
The pesticide was applied correctly at the right time
questions.why: Pests survive when the chemical does not reach them, is washed off, or is applied improperly.

questions.q: Using fewer pesticides lowers the risk that persistent chemicals contaminate groundwater.
questions.why: That is part of how IPM promotes a healthy environment.

questions.q: Name the five reasons to practice IPM.
questions.answer: It keeps a balanced ecosystem, pesticides can be ineffective, it saves money, it promotes a healthy environment, and it maintains a good public image.
questions.why: Balanced ecosystem, pesticides can be ineffective, saves money, healthy environment, good public image.

p: The components of an IPM approach can be grouped into the following five steps.

ol: Identify the pest and understand its biology.
Monitor the pest to be managed.

body.h: 1. Identify the pest and understand its biology

p: The first step in any pest management program is to identify the pest, whether you are dealing with an insect, weed, plant disease, or vertebrate animal.
Once you have identified the pest, you can determine its significance and the need for control.
Some pests have little impact on a plant, animal, or structure and do not require control.
Others warrant immediate control because they cause serious damage or present a significant threat to human health or public safety.
**Key pests** may cause major damage on a regular basis unless they are controlled.
Many weeds, for example, are key pests because they compete with crop or ornamental plants for resources and require regular control efforts to prevent or reduce damage.
Cockroaches and rodents are also examples of key pests because their waste and body coverings, shed cockroach skins and rodent hairs, can trigger **asthma** in some people.
**Secondary pests** become a problem when a key pest is controlled or absent.
For example, some weed species become pests only after key weeds, which are normally more successful in competing for resources, are controlled.
Certain species of fleas, ticks, and blood-feeding bugs attack people only when their natural hosts, such as pet dogs or cats, are no longer present.
**Occasional pests** become troublesome only once in a while because of their life cycles, environmental influences, or as a result of human activities.
For instance, ants may become occasional pests when sanitation practices change, providing them with food that previously did not exist.
They also may move into buildings after a rainfall or other event destroys an outdoor food source.

questions.q: A pest that may cause major damage on a regular basis unless it is controlled is called a:
questions.why: Key pests cause major damage on a regular basis unless controlled.

questions.q: After a family gives away their dog, fleas in the house start biting the people. What kind of pest are these fleas?
questions.why: Some fleas attack people only when their natural hosts, such as pet dogs or cats, are no longer present.

questions.q: Heavy rain destroys an outdoor food source, and ants move into a building. What kind of pest are the ants?
questions.why: Occasional pests become troublesome only once in a while, as when ants move in after rainfall.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the five components of IPM?
choices: Identify the pest and understand its biology
Spray on a regular calendar schedule
questions.why: The five: identify, monitor, develop the goal, implement, record and evaluate.

questions.q: List the five components of IPM, in order.
questions.answer: Identify the pest, monitor the pest, develop the pest management goal, implement the IPM program, and record and evaluate results.
questions.why: Identify, monitor, develop the goal, implement, record and evaluate.

sections.title: IPM step 2: monitoring, ET and EIL

p: The key to a successful IPM program is **regular monitoring**.
This involves measuring pest populations and/or the resulting damage or losses.
Monitoring procedures vary with the pest and the situation.
Carefully looking at plants or animals over time, called **scouting**, and **trapping** are often used to monitor insects and their activity.
**Weather and temperature data** are particularly helpful in following a pest's life cycle or in predicting how long it takes a certain pest to develop.
Models exist for specific insects and plant diseases that predict the need for and timing of pesticide applications.
Agricultural or ornamental producers must understand the concept of economic thresholds.
The presence of a pest does not always cause a loss in quality or quantity of a product.
To justify the cost of control, pest populations must be large enough to cause significant damage.
The **economic threshold (ET)** is the pest population density, the number of pests per unit area, at which control measures are needed to prevent the pest from reaching the economic injury level.
The **economic injury level (EIL)** is the pest population density that causes losses equal to the cost of control measures.
To justify using a control method, it is necessary to **set the ET below the EIL**.
Otherwise, producers lose money: first from the damage caused by the pest, and then by the cost of the control method.
Setting the ET below the EIL triggers the appropriate control method before pests reach the EIL.

figures.title: Figure 1.3: To make a control measure profitable, or at least break even, it is necessary to set the economic threshold below the economic injury level
explain: The pest population rises over time.
The time to treat is when the population reaches the economic threshold, the dashed line, which sits below the economic injury level.
The treated population falls before it reaches the economic injury level. The untreated population climbs past it.

questions.q: The economic injury level (EIL) is the pest population density that:
choices: Causes losses equal to the cost of control measures
questions.why: The EIL is the pest density where losses equal the cost of control.

questions.q: Where must the economic threshold (ET) be set?
questions.why: Setting the ET below the EIL triggers control before pests reach the EIL.

questions.q: A soybean grower waits to spray until the pest population reaches the economic injury level. What happens, according to the manual?
choices: The grower loses money, first from pest damage and then from the cost of control
The grower saves money by waiting
Nothing; that is the correct timing
questions.why: If the ET is not below the EIL, producers lose money from the damage and then from the control cost.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT described as part of monitoring pests?
questions.why: Scouting, trapping, and weather and temperature data are monitoring tools.

questions.q: What is the economic threshold (ET)?
questions.answer: The pest population density at which control measures are needed to prevent the pest from reaching the economic injury level.
questions.why: The ET is the pest density at which you act so the pest does not reach the EIL.

p: For pest managers not directly involved in commodity production, the concept of an **action threshold** is more appropriate.
An action threshold is the pest level at which some type of pest management action must be taken.
This is a **predetermined pest level that is deemed unacceptable**.
Often the action threshold is expressed as the number of pests per unit area.
Below this level, IPM practitioners do not use any control measures, though they should continue to monitor the situation and do sanitation inspections as needed.
Once a pest is at or above the action threshold, you should implement appropriate IPM strategies.
In some situations, the action threshold for a pest may be **zero**, meaning no presence of the pest is tolerated.
Examples include pests capable of transmitting a human pathogen, for example, mosquitoes and the **West Nile virus**, or of creating a public health emergency, for example, cockroaches or rodents.
In an urban landscape, action thresholds consider not only the economic value of the landscape but also its **ecological and aesthetic roles**.

A higher action threshold would be set for insect damage when no harm is done to the plant, for example, leaf galls on a shade tree, compared to a wood-borer that may destroy the tree, which has an action threshold of zero.
Action thresholds may vary **by pest**, for example, a stinging insect in a classroom versus a foraging ant.
They may vary **by site**, for example, a storage room versus a school infirmary.
And they may vary **by season**, for example, pests present daily versus two weeks of a year.
Establishing action thresholds for a new IPM program will require a practical approach.
First, establish an **arbitrary action threshold** for the major pests you encounter.
Then, **revise the action levels up or down** as you gain understanding of a specific pest management setting.

questions.q: Which statement about action thresholds is **true**?
choices: The IPM technician needs to implement control measures below the action threshold level.
The action threshold for a pest may be set at a zero pest population density.
In an urban landscape, action thresholds are usually more related to economics than aesthetics.
questions.ref: Review question 9, p. 18. Answer in the text: pp. 11–12, 'Pest Population Thresholds'
questions.why: A threshold can be zero. Below the threshold no controls are used, and urban thresholds weigh ecological and aesthetic roles too.

questions.q: What is an action threshold?
choices: The pest level at which some type of pest management action must be taken
The date pesticides must be applied
The level at which pests become resistant
questions.why: It is a predetermined pest level deemed unacceptable.

questions.q: Mosquitoes that can carry West Nile virus are found near a school. What action threshold does the manual describe for pests like this?
choices: Zero: no presence of the pest is tolerated
Very high, because mosquitoes are common
The same as for leaf galls on a shade tree
questions.why: Pests that can transmit a human pathogen can have an action threshold of zero.

questions.q: Leaf galls are on a shade tree but do no harm to it. Compared with a wood-borer that may destroy the tree, the action threshold for the galls should be:
questions.why: No harm to the plant means a higher threshold. The wood-borer's threshold is zero.

questions.q: Action thresholds may vary by all of these EXCEPT:
choices: The brand of pesticide on hand
questions.why: Thresholds vary by pest, by site, and by season.

questions.q: For a new IPM program, the manual says to first set an arbitrary action threshold for major pests, then revise it up or down as you learn.
questions.why: Establishing thresholds takes a practical approach: start arbitrary, then adjust.

sections.title: IPM step 3: the goal, and prevention

p: The goal of IPM programs is to keep pest damage at **economically or aesthetically acceptable levels**.
**Prevention** and **suppression** techniques are often combined in an effective IPM program.
Eradication is sometimes, though rarely, the goal.
The strategy for a sound IPM program is to coordinate the use of multiple tactics into a single integrated system.
Pesticides are just one control method.
**Nonchemical methods** may provide longer and more permanent pest control. **Consider these first** when developing a pest management strategy.
Evaluate the costs, benefits, and liabilities of each tactic.
There are economically and environmentally sound ways to prevent loss or damage from pests.
Such techniques include planting **weed- and disease-free seed** and growing varieties of plants **resistant** to diseases or insects.
Other choices are using cultural controls to prevent weedy plants from seeding, and choosing planting and harvesting times that lessen pest problems.
Sanitation methods often reduce pest buildup.
Other preventive methods involve **excluding pests** from the target area or host, and using practices that conserve natural enemies.
Making sure that plants, poultry, or livestock receive adequate water and nutrients often reduces stress and susceptibility to diseases or pests.
Pesticides are sometimes used for pest prevention.
For instance, growers treat some crops and landscapes with **preplant or preemergence herbicides** because they know that weed seeds are already present.
If plant pathogens have already infected susceptible plants, economic damage usually cannot be prevented.
For this reason, **fungicides are normally applied before infection occurs**, whenever environmental conditions favor infection.
Likewise, pesticides may be applied to **structural lumber before construction** to protect it from wood-destroying insects and fungi.

questions.q: Which statement about pest management strategies in IPM is **true**?
choices: The goal is to prevent pests from reaching damaging levels.
Eradication is never the goal of an IPM program.
Nonchemical methods are short-term solutions to control pests.
questions.ref: Review question 7, p. 17. Answer in the text: p. 10, IPM goal, and p. 12, 'Develop the pest management goal'
questions.why: Eradication is sometimes, though rarely, the goal, and nonchemical methods may give longer, more permanent control.

questions.q: What does the manual say to consider FIRST when developing a pest management strategy?
questions.why: Nonchemical methods may provide longer and more permanent control, so consider them first.

questions.q: A field gets a fungal disease almost every wet spring. When does the manual say fungicides are normally applied?
choices: Before infection occurs, whenever environmental conditions favor infection
Only after the disease is widespread
Never, because fungicides cannot prevent disease
questions.why: Once pathogens infect susceptible plants, economic damage usually cannot be prevented.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT listed as a preventive technique?
choices: Excluding pests from the target area or host
Releasing sterile insects over an infested region
questions.why: Releasing sterile insects is an eradication procedure.

questions.q: Preemergence herbicides are an example of using pesticides for prevention.
questions.why: Growers use preplant or preemergence herbicides because they know weed seeds are already present.

questions.q: What is the goal of IPM programs, according to step 3?
choices: Keep pest damage at economically or aesthetically acceptable levels
Use as many pesticides as possible
questions.why: The goal is to keep damage at economically or aesthetically acceptable levels.

sections.title: Suppression, eradication, and IPM steps 4 and 5

p: Suppressive pest control methods aim to **reduce pest population levels**.
These methods usually do not eliminate all pests but reduce their populations to a tolerable level or to a point **below the EIL**.
Suppression sometimes lowers pest populations so that natural enemies can maintain control.
**Suppression is the goal of most pesticide applications.**
Other techniques, such as cultivation, mowing weeds, and releasing biological control agents, are also used to suppress pest populations.
Eradication efforts are effective in **buildings or other small, confined spaces** where, once the pest is eliminated, it can be excluded.
For example, eliminating cockroaches, rats, and mice from **commercial food establishments** requires eradication.
Over larger areas, however, eradication is very expensive and often has limited success.
Regulatory eradication programs are usually directed at **exotic or introduced pests** posing an area-wide public health or economic threat.

body.h: 4. Implement the integrated pest management program

p: Once you have selected appropriate methods and have set predetermined thresholds, you can initiate the IPM program.
IPM programs are specific to each situation and can be adjusted as you learn more about the pest and the site.
Observe all local, state, and federal regulations regarding the methods chosen.
It is extremely important to **record and evaluate the results** of each pest management effort.
Some control methods, especially **nonchemical ones, are slow to yield measurable results**.
Other methods may be ineffective or even damage the target crop, animal, treated surface, or natural enemy.
Objectively evaluate how well your strategies work so that you will be better prepared if you must control a specific pest again.

questions.q: Which would be considered a preventive pest management strategy?
choices: Planting weed- and disease-free seed on an athletic field.
Releasing natural enemies to help reduce pest populations.
Removing a pest that is a public health concern from an area.
questions.ref: Review question 8, p. 17. Answer in the text: p. 12, 'Prevention'
questions.why: Clean seed is prevention. Releasing natural enemies suppresses, and removing a pest from an area is eradication.

questions.q: What is the goal of most pesticide applications?
questions.why: Suppression is the goal of most pesticide applications.

questions.q: A restaurant has cockroaches, rats, and mice. What goal does the manual say this situation requires?
questions.why: Eliminating cockroaches, rats, and mice from commercial food establishments requires eradication.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT true about eradication?
choices: It is effective in buildings and small, confined spaces
Over large areas it is very expensive and often has limited success
Regulatory eradication targets exotic or introduced pests
It is the goal of most pesticide applications
questions.why: Suppression, not eradication, is the goal of most pesticide applications.

questions.q: Some control methods, especially nonchemical ones, are slow to yield measurable results.
questions.why: That is one reason recording and evaluating results matters.

questions.q: Suppression reduces pest populations to a tolerable level or to a point below what?
questions.why: Suppression lowers populations to a tolerable level or below the EIL.

p: As noted earlier, pesticides represent only one tool in the IPM toolbox.
When combined with other control methods, they can help create an effective treatment plan to reduce pest populations.
However, pesticides might not control the pests as expected. A good pest manager needs to find out why.
**Pest identification.** Sometimes a pesticide application fails because the pest was not identified correctly.
Being able to accurately identify pests requires patience and practice.
For example, knowing the difference between a **caterpillar and a sawfly** will result in success or failure when using **Bacillus thuringiensis**.
Bt is effective on caterpillars but not on sawflies.
Even nonchemical tactics may fail if the pest and susceptible life stages are not accurately identified.
**Dosage.** Make sure that you have applied the correct pesticide at the correct dosage, according to label instructions.
**Correct use.** Some herbicides are formulated to kill grasses, others for broadleaf weeds, and still others can kill both types of weeds.
Always read the pesticide label to see if the target pest is listed.
**Application timing.** Other applications fail because the pesticide was not applied at the correct time.
The pest may not have been in the area during the application, or it may have been in a life cycle stage where it was not susceptible to the pesticide.
**Insects are usually more vulnerable when they are immature**, and **weeds are most easily controlled before they flower and go to seed**.
Also, remember that current pests may be part of a new infestation that developed long after the chemical was applied.
**Application equipment.** Concealed pests, under leaves or bark, in the soil, or within stems or fruits, are difficult to reach.
This means that knowing the best type of application equipment to use is very important.
For example, use an **air-blast sprayer** for pests hiding under apple tree leaves, but a **granular applicator** during planting operations for soil-dwelling agronomic pests.
**Environmental conditions.** In general, do not apply pesticides just before a **rainstorm**.
The pesticide may be washed off the target plants and away from the application site.
Temperature extremes and windy conditions can move pesticides away from the target pests and site.
**Pesticide degradation.** Pesticides may degrade when stored.
Under some conditions, pesticides can change into a form that is ineffective, due to the age of the product or the pesticide storage conditions.
For example, **granular pesticides stored in wet or very humid conditions** will draw moisture.
This may cause **clumping and possible deactivation** of the pesticide.

questions.q: A grower sprays Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) on larvae that turn out to be sawflies, and nothing dies. Why did it fail?
choices: The pest was misidentified; Bt works on caterpillars but not sawflies
Bt works only on adult insects
questions.why: Knowing a caterpillar from a sawfly decides success or failure with Bt.

questions.q: When are insects usually most vulnerable to pesticides?
questions.why: Insects are usually more vulnerable when they are immature.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the reasons the manual gives for pesticide application failure?
questions.why: The reasons: identification, dosage, correct use, timing, equipment, environmental conditions, degradation.

questions.q: Pests are hiding under apple tree leaves. Which equipment does the manual recommend?
questions.why: Air-blast sprayer for pests under apple leaves; granular applicator for soil-dwelling pests at planting.

questions.q: Granular pesticides stored in wet or very humid conditions draw moisture. What can this cause?
questions.answer: Clumping and possible deactivation of the pesticide
questions.why: Moisture can cause clumping and possible deactivation.

p: **Pesticide resistance** is the ability of a pest to tolerate a pesticide that once controlled it.
Resistance develops when intensive pesticide use kills the **susceptible individuals** in a population but leaves the **resistant ones to reproduce**.
Initially, **higher labeled rates and more frequent applications** are needed to control resistant pests.
Eventually the pesticide will have **little or no effect** on the pest population as the resistant population grows.
Resistance may develop to a single insecticide, fungicide, herbicide, or rodenticide.
More often, however, pest populations become resistant to **chemically related pesticides in a class of compounds**.
It is also possible for a pest to develop resistance to pesticides in two or more classes of compounds with different modes of action.

Continual use of pesticides from the **same chemical class**, such as all growth regulator herbicides or all pyrethroid insecticides, increases the likelihood that resistance will develop in a pest population.
**Frequent applications** and **greater persistence** of the chemical further increase the chances of pesticide resistance.

Finally, resistance can spread through a pest population much more rapidly in pests that have **many generations per year and many offspring per generation**, such as many insects, mites, fungi, and rodents.

figures.title: Figure 1.4: Pesticide resistance
explain: Panel 1: Some individuals in a pest population have genetic traits that allow them to survive pesticide application.
Panel 2: A proportion of the survivor's offspring inherit the resistance traits. At the next spraying these resistant individuals will survive.
Panel 3: If pesticides are applied frequently, the pest population will soon consist mostly of resistant individuals.

questions.q: Which would increase the likelihood of pesticide resistance?
choices: An insect that has one generation per year.
Continual use of pesticides from the same chemical class.
Applying a pesticide that has little or no residual effect.
questions.ref: Review question 10, p. 18. Answer in the text: p. 14, 'Pesticide Resistance'
questions.why: Many generations and greater persistence raise the chances, so A and C lower them.

questions.q: What is pesticide resistance?
choices: The ability of a pest to tolerate a pesticide that once controlled it
A pesticide that lasts a long time
The time it takes a pesticide to break down
questions.why: Resistance is a pest's ability to tolerate a pesticide that once controlled it.

questions.q: Which of these does NOT increase the chances of pesticide resistance?
choices: Continual use of pesticides from the same chemical class
Pests that have few generations per year and few offspring
questions.why: Many generations and many offspring speed resistance up. Few does not.

questions.q: A turf manager uses only pyrethroid insecticides, year after year. What does the manual say this does?
choices: Increases the likelihood that resistance will develop
Prevents resistance because pyrethroids are a single class
questions.why: Continual use of one chemical class, such as all pyrethroids, increases the likelihood of resistance.

questions.q: Resistance spreads much more rapidly in pests with many generations per year and many offspring per generation.
questions.why: Many insects, mites, fungi, and rodents fit this description.

questions.q: In the early stages of resistance, what happens?
choices: Higher labeled rates and more frequent applications are needed to control the pests
The pesticide stops working completely right away
The pests die faster than before
questions.why: First it takes higher rates and more applications; eventually the pesticide has little or no effect.

p: Several pest management tactics help **prevent or delay** the occurrence of pesticide resistance.
One approach is the use of **new or altered pesticides**.
Using new compounds with **different modes of action** will lessen the likelihood of resistance developing in a population.
Most pesticides have a **code number at the top of the label** indicating the mode of action, for example, **Group 4A Insecticides, Neonicotinoids**, or **Group 2 Herbicides, ALS Inhibitors**.
Unfortunately, new replacement products are often quite complex, difficult to synthesize, and very costly to develop.
Moreover, they have very specific modes of action, which can rapidly lead to the development of resistant pest populations even after limited use in the field.
No longer can we expect to respond to pesticide resistance by merely substituting one pesticide for another.
**Changing pesticide use patterns** is an important step in preventing resistance.
When **dosages are reduced**, fewer pests are killed, so the pressure to develop resistant pest populations is decreased.
**Applying pesticides over limited areas** reduces the proportion of the total pest population exposed to the chemical.
The result is a large pool of individuals still susceptible to the pesticide.

This tactic tends to delay the development of a resistant population because pesticide-susceptible individuals continue to interbreed with resistant ones, thus **diluting the resistance** in the population.
Also, **treating alternate generations** of pests with pesticides that have different modes of action decreases the selection pressure for resistance.
Managing pesticide resistance is a critical aspect of integrated pest management.
Monitor pest populations carefully and **treat only when necessary instead of on a schedule**.
Good pesticide **application records** are another important part of resistance management.
Pesticides are more effectively managed when **treatment history** is known.
Resistance must be **detected when it is at a very low level**.
It should then be controlled by using all available pest management techniques to extend the useful life of our current pesticides.

questions.q: Where do most pesticides show a code number for the mode of action?
choices: At the top of the label
questions.why: Examples: Group 4A Insecticides, Neonicotinoids, or Group 2 Herbicides, ALS Inhibitors.

questions.q: A grower wants to slow resistance. Which plan follows the manual?
choices: Treat alternate generations with pesticides that have different modes of action
Use the same pesticide at higher rates every week
Treat the whole area on a fixed schedule
Switch to a new product with the same mode of action
questions.why: Treating alternate generations with different modes of action decreases selection pressure.

questions.q: Which of these does NOT help delay resistance, according to the manual?
questions.why: Treat only when necessary instead of on a schedule.

questions.q: Why does applying pesticides over limited areas delay resistance?
choices: Susceptible individuals keep interbreeding with resistant ones, diluting the resistance
It kills every pest in the area
It lowers the cost of pesticides
questions.why: A large pool of susceptible pests remains, and they dilute the resistance.

questions.q: Using mode of action, what is one way to lessen the chance of resistance?
questions.answer: Use pesticides with different modes of action
questions.why: New compounds with different modes of action lessen the likelihood of resistance.

p: A successful pest management program begins with the **proper identification** of the pest.
Choosing the appropriate pest control method depends on recognizing and understanding the pest, its **life cycle, habits, and habitat**.
Integrated pest management programs attempt to balance the need for pest control with the desire to protect the environment from pesticide contamination.
**Monitoring** is critical to knowing where pests are located, when to act against growing pest populations, and what type of control measures to use.
Evaluation and recording results help to determine how well the IPM program is working and whether there are any harmful human or environmental effects.
Minimizing pesticide resistance is critical for sustaining the effectiveness of pest management programs.
Using a variety of tools and techniques will help prevent or delay the occurrence of pesticide resistance.
If the pest has not been properly identified, **even nonchemical control tactics will fail**.
It is your responsibility to consider the effects of pest control actions on the **entire treatment site**, whether an outdoor area or inside a structure.
Use good judgment, especially when pesticides are part of the control strategy, to avoid harmful effects to other living organisms and the environment.

questions.q: According to the chapter summary, a successful pest management program begins with:
questions.why: Everything else depends on knowing what the pest is.

questions.q: If a pest has not been properly identified, nonchemical control tactics will still work.
questions.why: Without proper identification, even nonchemical control tactics will fail.

questions.q: Monitoring helps you know all of these EXCEPT:
choices: When to act against growing pest populations
What type of control measures to use
questions.why: Monitoring tells you where pests are, when to act, and what control to use.

questions.q: You are treating a building for pests. Whose responsibility is it to consider the effects of the treatment on the entire treatment site?
questions.why: It is your responsibility, outdoors or inside a structure.
